exercises.approach: Trace the dispatch on both arguments: x and y are FormalMeasure objects, so the (FormalMeasure, FormalMeasure) method runs, validates both, compares units and builds a new object from `c(x@values, y@values)`.
exercises.why: Both units are "ms", so the method concatenates the observations in argument order, 1, 3 and then 5, and the new object passes validity again on construction.
exercises.wrong: Expecting arithmetic. `c(1, 3) + 5` recycles the 5 and gives 6 and 8, but combine_measure joins observations; it never adds them.

exercises.approach: Build `seconds <- new("FormalMeasure", values = 2, unit = "s")` and call `combine_measure(x, seconds)` inside a handler that expects "incompatible units".
exercises.why: Both arguments are still FormalMeasure objects, so the same method is selected; dispatch looks at classes, not slot contents. The `identical(x@unit, y@unit)` check inside the method is what rejects ms against s.
exercises.wrong: Expecting dispatch to choose another method or to convert. Without the unit check the result would be 1, 3 and 2 labeled ms, treating two seconds as two milliseconds, an error by a factor of 1000.

exercises.approach: Call `new("FormalMeasure", values = Inf, unit = "ms")` and capture the error message.
exercises.why: The slot type is numeric and Inf is numeric, so the slot check passes. new() then runs the function registered with setValidity, which finds a nonfinite value and returns its message, so construction stops.
exercises.wrong: Relying on `slots = c(values = "numeric")` as the guard. Inf, negative Inf and NaN are all numeric, so a type-only class would accept them and every later total would be infinite or NaN.
exercises.verify: The captured message contains "values must be a finite vector" after the invalid class prefix.

exercises.approach: After a direct slot assignment, call `validObject(broken)` before the object leaves the code that changed it, and prefer a replacement function that validates for callers.
exercises.why: `@<-` checks only that the new value has the slot's class. character(0) is character, so the assignment succeeds, and only the validity function notices that the unit is not one string.
exercises.wrong: Assuming `@<-` runs validity. Code that reads `broken@unit` without validating gets a zero-length value, and `paste(2, broken@unit)` quietly returns "2 " with the unit missing.
exercises.verify: `tryCatch(validObject(broken), error = conditionMessage)` returns a message containing "unit must be one nonempty string".

exercises.approach: Call `combine_measure(x, 2)` on its own and assert its specific message, separately from the unit mismatch test.
exercises.why: The signature (FormalMeasure, numeric) matches exactly, so that method runs and stops with "numeric input has no declared unit". It is a different branch from the mismatch check, so it needs its own test.
exercises.wrong: Treating the bare 2 as milliseconds because x is in ms. If that method were missing, dispatch would fail with a missing method error, and a test that matched any error would pass for the wrong reason.
exercises.verify: `tryCatch(combine_measure(x, 2), error = conditionMessage)` returns "numeric input has no declared unit".

exercises.approach: Write `to_ms()` to validate its input, require unit "s", multiply the values by 1000 and construct a new FormalMeasure with unit "ms".
exercises.why: A conversion must change values and unit together. Building a new object runs validity again, and the input is never modified, so 2 seconds becomes 2000 ms while seconds still holds 2 and "s".
exercises.wrong: Changing only the unit with `seconds@unit <- "ms"`. That relabels 2 as 2 ms, wrong by a factor of 1000, and the same mistake repeats if a ms object is converted without the unit check.
exercises.verify: `to_ms(seconds)@values` returns 2000, `seconds@values` still returns 2, and `to_ms(x)` stops with "conversion requires seconds".

run_note: The starter supplies values 1 and 3, a second value of 5 and the unit ms, with one TODO per exercise. Run it, then define the class with a validity function that checks both slots together. Exercise 4 assigns an empty unit through `@` directly, which skips validity, so plan to call `validObject()` yourself to expose the broken invariant.
checks_note: The assertions confirm that invalid construction fails with the expected diagnostic, that combining 1 and 3 ms with 5 ms gives values 1, 3 and 5 in ms, and that converting 2 seconds yields 2000 ms while the original seconds object still holds 2 s. They do not prove that every method signature validates units, only the combinations exercised here.
